transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (CTO, Evergreen), Janelle Park (Head of Data), Owen Li (Platform Eng), Sophie Allen (Security)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on integration options for Redwood (hosted vs dedicated vs private), SDK support, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, routing via gateway/proxy, rate limits and quotas, and observability hooks (tracing, logs, token-level cost breakdown). Customer is evaluating for a pilot tied to their recommender/chat features and needs clarity on feasibility, security, and cost.

[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Ava on the account team, Daniel and Priya are our SEs. Mark, want to kick us off with what you're trying to solve?

[00:17] Mark Rivera: Sure. Thanks Ava. We're Evergreen Retail, marketplace + in-store pickup biz. We have a couple of initiatives — personalized product recs, customer support chat, and on-site search augmentation. We're evaluating Redwood because we've heard good things about your latency/cost story and the dedicated/private options. Today we want to understand integration effort and security posture.

[00:37] Daniel Cho: Great. Can you describe current stack and where you'd want Redwood to sit? Are you building directly into our API or through an internal gateway?

[00:45] Janelle Park: Our stack is mostly AWS. API layer on ECS with internal Kong gateway, Kafka for events, and a mix of Python/Node microservices. We already use LangChain in a couple of PoCs and are experimenting with LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented generation. Ideally Redwood would be called from a service behind our gateway, but we also want to explore direct server-side SDKs.

[01:06] Daniel Cho: Good, that's a common pattern. Redwood supports server SDKs for Python, Node, and Java. We also have first-class compatibility with LangChain and an adapter for LlamaIndex — sample notebooks we can share. For gateway setups, you can either route traffic from your gateway to Redwood's hosted endpoints, or if you want private deployment we can do VPC peering or a private control plane that sits behind your network.

[01:30] Owen Li: Important for us: we have strict egress rules and prefer not to open too many outbound connections from our prod VLAN. How does VPC/private deployment work?

[01:40] Priya Singh: For Private we support an on-prem or VPC-connected private control plane. You manage network egress; we provide an appliance or containerized control plane that you run in your VPC with optional private endpoints to Redwood runtime. Alternatively, Dedicated can be deployed in your cloud account with reserved GPU pools and private networking. We can go over the KMS/HSM integration for key management as well.

[01:58] Sophie Allen: From security side, we need SOC 2, SSO (SAML/Okta), RBAC, audit logs, and customer-managed keys. Also data residency in the EU for some segments. Do you have those?

[02:12] Ava Martinez: Yes — we are SOC 2 Type II, support SAML SSO integrations (Okta, Azure AD), RBAC at org/team level, and audit logging. For KMS, we support customer-managed keys via cloud KMS integrations and HSM in Private deployments. We also offer region pinning for hosted so data doesn't leave chosen regions. We'll share the security pack after this call.

[02:31] Mark Rivera: Great. On the integration side, how opinionated are your SDKs? We run LangChain wrappers and also a custom in-house agent orchestrator. We don't want to rewrite a ton.

[02:42] Daniel Cho: Our SDKs are intentionally thin. They implement standard completion/chat/embeddings endpoints. LangChain has a Redwood LLM wrapper that looks like other LLM classes; it supports streaming and callbacks. For LlamaIndex we have a connector for storing and retrieving indexed nodes and using Redwood generation. For your orchestrator, you can call our REST API or use SDKs — both work. We provide a proxy pattern example so you can centralize auth and quota enforcement at your gateway.

[03:08] Janelle Park: About rate limiting — we have per-tenant throttles in our gateway and also want per-route limits against Redwood. How do quotas and rate limits look? Any burst handling?

[03:20] Priya Singh: You can set both account-level quotas and route-level policies. Hosted customers get API rate limits and quotas we enforce; for Dedicated, you control capacity via reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policies. We also support burst capacity for sustained traffic spikes. The runtime has graceful degradation: you can configure fallbacks (cheaper model or cached response) if capacity is saturated.

[03:41] Owen Li: If a request hits rate limits, do you get standard 429s? And does the SDK surface retry/backoff guidance?

[03:49] Daniel Cho: Yes, 429s for throttles with headers indicating retry-after. Our official SDKs include automatic retry/backoff strategies configurable per-client. For high-throughput, we recommend client-side batching and the prefix caching we provide to reduce token counts.

[04:06] Mark Rivera: We care about observability — tracing, token-level cost, and per-request latency. How do we hook into that?

[04:15] Priya Singh: Redwood Console gives per-request traces, token breakdown and cost per call, and per-model dashboards. For deeper integration we expose traces via OpenTelemetry and can forward logs to destinations like Datadog or Sumo. You can also emit request ids from your gateway and we surface them in logs so you can correlate.

[04:34] Sophie Allen: Can we ship audit logs to our SIEM and retain them for 12 months?

[04:39] Ava Martinez: For Dedicated/Private, you can configure log forwarding to your SIEM and set retention policies. Hosted customers have standard retention tiers, and we offer add-on extended retention for enterprise. We'll include the retention matrix in the security docs.

[04:52] Janelle Park: On the developer experience, how easy is it to prototype with LangChain/LlamaIndex and then move to production? We hate getting stuck in PoC tech debt.

[05:03] Daniel Cho: We recommend prototyping against Hosted (rapid onboarding) using our SDK with LangChain adapters. Once you validate prompts and models, you can pin specific model versions and move to Dedicated or Private for predictable latency and data controls. We have migration guides and a rollout mechanism — canary or A/B — to shift traffic while maintaining consistent API contracts.

[05:24] Mark Rivera: Any gotchas around tokenization or model differences when moving between hosted and dedicated?

[05:30] Priya Singh: Model behavior is consistent for same model families, but you may pick a quantized variant for Dedicated to save costs which can slightly change tokenization/perplexity. We provide evaluation tooling and automatic quality regression checks tied to your prompt sets so you can compare results before cutting over.

[05:48] Sophie Allen: On encryption — do you encrypt data in transit and at rest by default? And how about customer-managed keys for hosted?

[05:56] Ava Martinez: All traffic is TLS. At rest encryption is default; for hosted we provide customer-managed keys via KMS integrations for enterprise accounts. For Private, you manage the keys in your environment.

[06:07] Janelle Park: We run some heavy retrievals — about 6k token requests per session peak. For cost purposes we want to compute an estimated cost per 1M tokens. How do we do that with your pricing?

[06:17] Ava Martinez: I'll send the hosted vs dedicated pricing sheet. Roughly, hosted per-token price depends on model; Dedicated is more of reserved capacity with lower per-token economics if you hit utilization targets. For heavy RAG workloads, caching and batching and smaller context models for embeddings can cut cost a lot. We'll include a sample calc in the follow-up.

[06:34] Owen Li: For gateway pattern: our plan is to have an internal proxy that adds auth and tenant-id header, does rate-limiting and logging and then forwards to Redwood. We want the ability to throttle per-tenant and to track per-tenant spend. Is there support for passing tenant metadata?

[06:50] Daniel Cho: Yes, you can pass metadata headers (we recommend a signed tenant header) and we surface that in console and billing reports. For Dedicated you can also create sub-accounts or API keys per-tenant and apply quotas.

[07:05] Mark Rivera: A concrete question — we use LlamaIndex for vector stores and orchestration. Does Redwood host vector DBs or do you expect us to manage them?

[07:15] Priya Singh: We don't host a general-purpose vector DB, but we integrate with common stores (Pinecone, Milvus, Elasticsearch). The typical pattern is you host the index and use Redwood for embeddings + generation. We can help with connector examples and provide guidelines on embedding model selection and sharding for latency.

[07:32] Janelle Park: Are there examples or sample repos for LangChain + Redwood + our gateway?

[07:37] Daniel Cho: Yes. We'll share two repos: a LangChain notebook with a Redwood LLM wrapper and a gateway-proxy example that shows auth, tenant headers, retry logic, and quota enforcement. We'll also include a LlamaIndex integration notebook.

[07:49] Sophie Allen: For the security review, do you have a standard questionnaire or an intake form we can fill before our security call?

[07:56] Ava Martinez: Yes, we have a security questionnaire and SOC2 pack. I'll send the intake form; once you fill it we'll set up a security deep-dive with our security lead.

[08:06] Mark Rivera: Timeline — we're targeting a pilot by end of May. The pilot would be product recs on web and a limited production chat feature. Is that realistic?

[08:16] Daniel Cho: Yes, that's realistic. Typical cadence: quick hosted pilot in 2-3 weeks for the PoC, then move to Dedicated if you need capacity and data isolation for production. We'll help with a benchmark run to validate latency and token costs.

[08:29] Janelle Park: For the benchmark, can you run a synthetic test with our prompt set and measure p50/p95 latency and token-per-call?

[08:36] Priya Singh: Absolutely. We'll need a sample prompt set and an expected traffic profile. We'll run both hosted and dedicated runs and return a spreadsheet with latency, throughput, and cost estimates.

[08:47] Owen Li: Ok, let's talk about fallback strategies. If Redwood runtime is saturated or there's a regional outage, can we fallback to a secondary model or another provider?

[08:57] Daniel Cho: Yes, we support smart routing rules. You can configure policies to route to cheaper/compatible model variants, different region, or an alternate provider. Our SDK exposes status codes and we have hooks for client-side fallback logic.

[09:12] Mark Rivera: Any advice on prompt engineering for cost control?

[09:18] Daniel Cho: Shorter contexts, reuse embeddings for context, use retrieval-first patterns, and leverage prefix/KV caching for common prompts. Also consider model selection: cheaper smaller models for non-critical text, larger ones for higher quality where necessary.

[09:31] Janelle Park: One more — observability hooks. Do you expose per-token attribution in traces?

[09:37] Priya Singh: We show token counts per call, token cost breakdown, and timeline for model stages. For deeper observability, you can attach request metadata and we emit structured logs and OpenTelemetry spans you can ingest.

[09:49] (short cross-talk about Slack integration and reference apps)

[10:05] Ava Martinez: Quick recap and next steps — we'll: 1) send pricing + dedicated sizing template, 2) share LangChain/LlamaIndex sample repos and gateway-proxy example, 3) send security pack + SOC2 docs + intake form, 4) provision a trial api key and start a benchmark once you send prompts. Anything to add?

[10:26] Mark Rivera: That covers it. Sophie will collate security questions and Owen will coordinate prompts and stakeholders. We'll aim to have the intake form back by Friday.

[10:36] Sophie Allen: Yes, I'll compile the list and send it. Also please include retention options for logs in the security pack.

[10:42] Ava Martinez: Noted. We'll follow up with calendar invite for the tech deep-dive. Thanks all.

[10:50] End of transcript (approx 52 minutes).
